q: How much CSF is produced each day?
why: About 500 ml/day is produced by the choroid plexus; total volume is about 150 ml.

q: Hydrocephalus from aqueduct stenosis is classified as what?
why: Obstruction within the ventricular system is non-communicating; blocked arachnoid villi (e.g. after SAH) cause communicating hydrocephalus.

why: Hakim’s triad describes normal pressure hydrocephalus.

q: At what level is an external ventricular drain zeroed?
o: The foramen of Monro (roughly the external auditory meatus when supine)
why: EVDs are zeroed at the foramen of Monro; drainage is level-dependent.

q: Which step of VP shunt insertion is most stimulating?
why: Tunnelling is very stimulating; deepen anaesthesia or boost remifentanil beforehand.

q: A child with a blocked shunt is vomiting and drowsy. How should anaesthesia be induced?
why: Vomiting means full stomach; plan an RSI and avoid hypercapnia and hypertension.

q: When is a VP shunt usually considered instead of continuing an external ventricular drain?
o: If an EVD is needed for more than about 10 days
why: A VP shunt is considered if drainage is needed beyond about 10 days; the distal end usually lies in the peritoneum.

q: What LP opening pressure is consistent with idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
why: An opening pressure over 25 cmH2O is diagnostic and draining CSF can be therapeutic; treatment includes acetazolamide and weight loss.

q: Which organism causes most spinal epidural abscesses?
why: About 80–90% are Staph aureus; urgent MRI and decompression are needed before deficits become irreversible.
